title: Label each part as it is named
statement: Put each label beside the part it names, with a short leader line, at the moment the narration names it, never in a legend or caption bar.
example: Across 50 studies, spatial and temporal contiguity improved learning by d = 0.85.
detail: A visual design guide for grade-7 science videos puts each one-to-three-word term beside its referent with a short leader line and never uses a legend or caption bar as the labelling system, because a legend makes the learner hold a colour or number in memory, search for its match and then return to the explanation (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-visuals-human-v0.1.md`, lines 86-98 and 256). It cites spatial and temporal contiguity at d=0.85 across 50 studies (Ginns 2006) and integrated text-in-diagram at g=0.63 (Schroeder & Cenkci 2018). Its examples count a bottom caption bar listing numbered parts as a defect, and likewise a label that appears after the narration has moved on (lines 95-98 and 315-316).
against: The guide's timing tolerances, a label within half a second of its first mention and a mismatch of more than a second counted as a defect, are production thresholds rather than study results (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-visuals-human-v0.1.md`, line 257).

evidence.quote: **Evidence.** Spatial and temporal contiguity produced *d*=0.85 across 50 studies [12]; integrated text-in-diagram produced *g*=0.63 [13].
Put each 1–3-word term beside its referent with a short leader line; never use a legend or caption bar as the labeling system.
A legend makes the learner hold a color or number in memory, search for its match, and then return to the explanation.
A label appearing before or after the moment its part is named.
The evidence supports contiguity; these tolerances are production thresholds.
